## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

According to its traditional frame narrative, the Buddha recounted this story while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with a mendicant with vagrant inclinations, beginning with the opening phrase, “Lo, my elephants”.

In studies of early Buddhist perspectives on conflict, the *Palāyitajātaka* is cited alongside Jātaka 181 and Jātaka 230 as a narrative illustrating the valorization of capturing an enemy alive (*jīvagrāham*) or prevailing over opponents through psychological intimidation rather than bloodshed [Jerryson and Juergensmeyer 2010].

 While DharmaNexus reports no cross-language parallels with a similarity score of 10 or greater, it identifies four Pali-internal matching segments (totaling 596 characters) shared between the canonical text and the commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), with the longest match aligning §1.1–2.4 to commentary segments §1382_4–1388 at a similarity of 0.96 [DharmaNexus].
